parent: Roman Health Ventures Inc. (trading as Ro). The terms of use name its affiliates Roman Health Medical LLC and Roman Health Pharmacy LLC (docs: https://ro.co/terms-of-use/, checked 2026-11-23).
model: US direct-to-patient telehealth company: an online questionnaire ('online visit') reviewed by a US-licensed clinician, with its own pharmacy shipping generic, off-label and compounded hair-loss medicines on quarterly or longer subscriptions.

access.accountWall: Men (start.ro.co/fxdxbh): after 3 marketing questions, on screen qid 55, an email pop-up ('See how much fuller your hair could be in just 3 months', email + two consent boxes, or Continue with Google) that cannot be dismissed. Women (start.ro.co/tefcyb): after 3 or 4 hair questions, on screen qid 16 'Thanks for sharing. Ready to go deeper?' (Sign up with Email / Continue with Google). Topical minoxidil, shampoo and conditioner: sign-up is the first or second screen. In every flow the wall comes before any medical question and before any recommendation.
blockers: Account wall before every medical question, so no branch after the wall could be replayed live.
No bot protection problem: the site and the consultation app load normally in the walker.
access.coverageNote: Stages 1 to 3. LIVE: every question that can be reached without an account was replayed with one answer changed at a time (21 replays in stage 2: men 3 questions, women 4), and three direct-purchase entries were opened in stage 1. Every replay ended at the account wall with no product or price shown. CODE: the consultation app itself downloads the complete question schema for each flow (every question, option, fork rule and variable change behind the wall) and the men's recommendation function is in a public JS chunk. Stage 2 ran those definitions through an offline simulator, one change at a time (291 simulated runs: 161 men, 130 women, saved in runs/sim/), which is where every post-wall rule and recommendation comes from. These are labelled 'code', not 'observed'. No email, phone, name or other contact detail was entered, nothing was submitted, no photo or payment was given. Honest note: on the first answer the page itself creates an anonymous draft visitor record and posts each answer to it; that is the site's normal anonymous behaviour, and each live replay leaves one such draft. Stage 3 (independent check, 23-24 Nov 2026): 18 more live replays (both baselines, every remaining pre-wall option, three combinations, the coupon link, two alternative entry links and the three direct-purchase links); all matched the recorded results. The served schemas (men v77, women v32) were unchanged; the recommender chunk was byte-identical; the new main bundle was re-read.

engineSummary: Ro runs two different engines, and both can be read in full from code the site serves to any visitor. MEN: a 'soft steer' engine. Three marketing questions, then an email wall, then the medical questionnaire (the baseline man passes 19 screens up to the recommendation; reporting past treatments or conditions adds follow-ups). Nothing medical stops a man (only age under 18, female sex or an unserved zip code). Answers switch on up to three 'do not recommend' flags, one per treatment. A fixed priority list (Ro Mane Spray, then finasteride 1 mg tablets, then oral minoxidil 2.5 mg tablets) makes the first unflagged treatment the 'recommended' one, but all three stay on the screen and can be picked, on a default quarterly plan, and a clinician decides afterwards. In the offline one-change sweep the compounded spray, the dearest product, was recommended for every profile except: finasteride-type worries (depression, anxiety, erectile dysfunction, trying for a baby, past finasteride problems) which move the pick to oral minoxidil; prostate cancer or a topical allergy, which move it to finasteride tablets; and five 'another diagnosis?' answers (patches, very sudden onset, scalp redness, past steroid injections, persistently low blood pressure) which remove the recommendation but not the products. Heart and blood-pressure red flags only flag the minoxidil tablet, so the minoxidil spray stays recommended. Goals, severity and pattern only personalise a recap screen. WOMEN: a 'gate' engine. Three or four hair questions, then the sign-up wall, then the medical questionnaire (the baseline woman passes 31 screens up to the product choice). Pregnancy, any diagnosed scalp condition, signs of virilisation, lupus or autoimmune disease, past scalp steroid injections and minoxidil allergy end the visit with a referral. Breastfeeding, cardiovascular conditions, high blood pressure and age 66+ remove the tablet and leave only the compounded topical. Everyone else chooses between oral minoxidil ($30 a month) and Hair Solution Rx ($40 a month), with 'No preference' defaulting to the tablet; pattern, severity and symptoms never change the options. Before either wall the answers change only the wording or number of the next question (observed live); no product or price appears. Non-prescription products (5% minoxidil solution, shampoo, conditioner) are sold through separate links with no questions.
strengths: Very short path to sign-up (3 to 4 easy questions) with the long medical questionnaire kept until after the email is captured; 21 live replays never showed a dead end before the wall.
One clear recommended product with the alternatives still visible and pickable, and the clinician as the final check: simple for the patient and it protects conversion.

Men's safety questions for oral minoxidil are detailed: blood-pressure follow-ups with a picture of the ranges, timed heart attack, stroke and bypass questions, arrhythmia types, resting heart rate, fainting.

Finasteride-specific steering is thoughtful: depression, anxiety, erectile dysfunction and trying for a baby all move the recommendation away from both finasteride products, with a plain caution screen about fertility.

Women's visit has firm, explained stop screens (pregnancy, scarring and autoimmune alopecias, virilisation signs) with a find-a-dermatologist link, plus scalp photos and tracked outcome scores (severity, confidence, stress).
Clear public price for every plan length; coupons (35% or 50% off the first order) attach silently from ad links; no charge until a clinician approves.
A broad men's range for a telehealth brand: licensed tablet, off-label oral minoxidil, a compounded 3-in-1 spray, OTC minoxidil, shampoo and conditioner.
weaknesses: The men's recommendation barely uses the consultation: the same product (the highest-priced compounded spray) is recommended to every unflagged man whatever his goals, pattern or severity, including a man who reports no hair loss yet.
No product, price or eligibility signal before the email wall; the wall pop-up cannot be closed. 'Seems too expensive' and 'Nervous about side effects' get no answer.

Men are never stopped: patches, very sudden loss, scalp inflammation, liver failure and stage 5 kidney disease all reach checkout, relying entirely on the clinician; pain, pus bumps and eyebrow loss do not even remove the recommendation.

Inconsistent logic visible in the schema: heart failure or angina flags the minoxidil tablet but leaves the 6% minoxidil spray recommended; prostate cancer steers towards finasteride tablets; 'finasteride tablets were not effective' still recommends the finasteride spray.
The men's visit has no scalp-photo step (only identity photos) and no family-history question, although the FAQ says photos are requested.

Women's product choice ignores pattern and severity, and 'No preference' defaults to the oral, off-label tablet with a boxed warning. Self-reported bald patches, scalp rash or sudden onset do not stop or redirect a woman; only a named diagnosis does.

No finasteride, spironolactone or other anti-androgen route for women (for example after the menopause), and no pathway at all for pregnant or breastfeeding-ineligible patients beyond 'see someone else'.
Public pages disagree with each other (the hair-loss FAQ still says finasteride is the only prescription option; the women's page says billed every 2 months while pricing says quarterly).
The whole engine, including every clinical branch and flag, is downloadable by anyone, which makes it easy to copy and easy to game.
opportunities: Show an indicative recommendation and price before asking for an email: Ro asks 3 questions and then walls everything.

A recommendation that visibly uses what was asked (pattern, severity, goals, tablet-or-topical preference, budget) instead of one fixed product order; explain why this product was chosen for this person.
Ask the patient's own preference (tablet, topical, 'no finasteride', 'no prescription') up front: Ro's men's flow never asks it and infers it only from medical flags.
Explained 'see a doctor first' screens for red-flag hair loss in men (patches, sudden loss, inflamed scalp), as Ro already does for women, and a useful hand-off rather than a dead end.
A licensed-product-first pathway (finasteride 1 mg, minoxidil 5%) with compounded products as a clearly explained second step; Ro leads with the compounded spray.
Flexible plans: Ro's hair products start at quarterly billing; a monthly or pause-any-time plan and a visible price before sign-up would stand out.
Better women's offer: a pathway by life stage (post-partum shedding, perimenopause, PCOS) with blood-test prompts, rather than one choice between two minoxidil products.
Use scalp photos and family history for men, and tell patients how the photo changed the plan.
Budget and side-effect worries are captured by Ro and then ignored: answer them directly (cheapest effective option, side-effect rates, topical-only route).

limitations: Nothing after the account wall was seen live. Every post-wall question, rule and recommendation comes from the served schema, the public recommender chunk and an offline simulation of them (evidence 'code'). The real screens may differ in small ways.

Live one-change testing was only possible on 7 questions (men q20, q22, q26, q28; women q4, q6, q8, q10). After stage 3 every option of those 7 questions has been replayed live, plus some multi-select combinations (men q20 all goals, q22 both 'tried' boxes; women q8 top + temples, temples + frontal). The alternative entry links were opened twice each (stages 1 and 3) and the coupon link twice; the paid-search quiz pages were read, not replayed.
What the clinician actually prescribes, how often the patient's pick is overridden, and which strengths are used after the first order cannot be known from public information.

Server-side checks (drug-interaction checks on the medicine list, state rules for compounded products, identity checks, the redirect flag for women entering the men's visit) are only visible as flags and function names; the list of states without the spray is not public.

The meaning of the answer marks ('negative', 'caution', 'ack-clinical') is inferred. They are saved with each answer on the server (seen in the anonymous add-answers responses), but who sees them was not found.

The variable isEligibleFor6And12MonthShipments (set when a man has used oral minoxidil or finasteride tablets before) is not used in the bundles read, so its effect on plan lengths is inferred, not shown.
The women's product catalogue (exact tablet strength, other plan lengths) is not fetched before the wall; women's strengths and prices come from schema text and the pricing page.
Free-text and searchable-list answers (medicines, allergies, other conditions) have no rule in the schema; any effect they have happens at clinician review.
The site runs A/B experiments and changes schema versions (men v77, women v32 on the check date); the three-product men's recommender is at 100% today.
Prices are US dollars and US plan structures; legal categories are US ones (Rx, OTC, compounded), not UK ones.
